name: Chin Hong Ming
bio: Chin Hong Ming was a Chinese-American convicted in federal court in New York in 1954 under the Trading With the Enemy Act for sending money to relatives in the People's Republic of China. His prosecution was one of a wave that treated ordinary family remittances as trading with a wartime enemy.
charges: Trading With the Enemy Act — for sending money to family in the People's Republic of China.

name: Chin You Gon
bio: Chin You Gon was a Chinese-American convicted in New York in 1954 under the Trading With the Enemy Act for remitting money to relatives in the People's Republic of China. The Chinese-American left press treated the prosecutions as ethnic and political persecution.
charges: Trading With the Enemy Act — for sending money to family in People's China.

name: Tom Sung
bio: Tom Sung was a Chinese-American prosecuted in New York in 1954 under the Trading With the Enemy Act for sending money to relatives in the People's Republic of China. He was convicted but received a suspended sentence.
charges: Trading With the Enemy Act — for remittances to family in People's China.

name: Fred Barreras
bio: Fred Barreras was a member of Mine-Mill Local 890 jailed for 90 days for defying an anti-picketing injunction during the 1950s Empire Zinc strike at Bayard, New Mexico — the strike dramatized in the film Salt of the Earth. Mexican-American miners and their families sustained the picket line in defiance of the courts.
charges: Criminal contempt — for defying an anti-picketing injunction during the Empire Zinc strike.

name: Cipriano Montoya
bio: Cipriano Montoya was a Mine-Mill Local 890 member jailed for 90 days for honoring the picket line during the Empire Zinc strike at Bayard, New Mexico. The strike and its mass arrests became the basis of the blacklisted film Salt of the Earth.
charges: Criminal contempt — for defying an anti-picketing injunction during the Empire Zinc strike.

name: Ernest Velasquez
bio: Ernest Velasquez was a strike leader of Mine-Mill Local 890 jailed for 90 days during the Empire Zinc strike at Bayard, New Mexico, for defying the anti-picketing injunction. The Mexican-American local's long strike inspired Salt of the Earth.
charges: Criminal contempt — for defying an anti-picketing injunction during the Empire Zinc strike.

name: Wil Ackalitis
bio: Wil Ackalitis was a New York longshoreman jailed for contempt in 1954 for his part in leading an International Longshoremen's Association strike on the waterfront. The dock strikes of the period were met with injunctions and contempt jailings.
charges: Contempt — for leading an ILA waterfront strike.

name: Harold Bowers
bio: Harold Bowers was a New York ILA longshore leader jailed for six months for contempt in 1954 over his role in a waterfront strike. The prosecutions accompanied the government drive against the dock unions.
charges: Contempt — for leading an ILA waterfront strike.

name: William Lynch
bio: William Lynch was a New York longshoreman jailed for contempt in 1954 for his part in an International Longshoremen's Association strike. He drew a three-month term.
charges: Contempt — for leading an ILA waterfront strike.

name: Bert Salwen
bio: Bert Salwen was a Communist Party candidate ruled off the New Jersey ballot in 1954 under the new Communist Control Act, which sought to outlaw the party outright. He challenged the exclusion as a denial of political rights.
charges: Barred from the ballot under the Communist Control Act of 1954.

name: Arnold Bernardini
bio: Arnold Bernardini was arrested for disorderly conduct while picketing in Brooklyn in November 1954 — one of the routine arrests used against union organizers on the picket line.

name: William Daley
bio: William Daley was arrested at the United Nations in 1954 and committed to the Bellevue psychiatric ward for protesting the U.S.-backed overthrow of the Arbenz government in Guatemala. Psychiatric confinement of a political protester drew condemnation as an abuse.
charges: Disorderly conduct — for protesting the U.S. role in Guatemala at the UN.
convicted: Arrested and sent to a psychiatric ward.

name: Reuel Amdur
bio: Reuel Amdur was convicted in Berkeley for setting up a sidewalk table without a permit to gather clemency signatures for the Rosenbergs — a permit he was denied because of his views. His conviction was overturned on appeal in 1954.
charges: Permit violation — for a sidewalk table collecting Rosenberg-clemency signatures.

name: Ammon Hennacy
bio: Ammon Hennacy was a Christian-anarchist pacifist — later a mainstay of the Catholic Worker movement — who was imprisoned in the Atlanta federal penitentiary during World War I for refusing to register for the draft, spending much of his term in solitary confinement. His 1917 imprisonment was recounted in the National Guardian in 1954.
charges: Refusing to register for the draft (World War I).
sentence: About two years, much of it in solitary confinement.
